_readme: The source registry is the moat. Anyone can scrape one directory; the value is in resolving the same operator across twenty sources and knowing which field to trust when they disagree. `trust` drives conflict resolution in identity-graph.ts: when two sources disagree on a field, the higher trust wins and the loser is kept as an alternate rather than discarded.

_access_modes.api: Official API under the provider's terms, with a key and a rate limit.
_access_modes.public-record: Government record, open by statute. Bulk files or an open portal.
_access_modes.licensed: Paid data licence or a subscription with contractual terms.
_access_modes.partner-required: No public API. Needs a commercial agreement before ingest — do not scrape it in the meantime.
_access_modes.first-party: Data the customer supplies or generates inside the product.

_retention_warning: retentionDays is a contractual ceiling, not a preference. Google Places allows place_id indefinitely but most other fields for 30 days; Yelp is 24 hours. That shapes the architecture: cache the identifier, store your own derived scores, re-fetch the vendor's content on read. Building a permanent copy of either would breach the terms and get the key pulled, which takes the product down for every customer at once.

sources.name: Google Places
sources.retentionException: place_id may be stored indefinitely and is the join key.
sources.notes: Best coverage and freshest hours of any discovery source. Billed per request, so it is the main variable cost — cache hard against place_id.

sources.name: Yelp Fusion
sources.notes: Strong on consumer-facing trades, thin on B2B and industrial. 24-hour retention ceiling means it is a live lookup, never a warehouse.

sources.name: OpenStreetMap
sources.notes: Free, unlimited, and the only free source of building footprints. ODbL is share-alike on a derived database — attribution is required and redistributing raw extracts carries obligations. Scores derived from it do not.

sources.name: Secretary of State filings
sources.notes: The highest-trust identity source in the whole registry, and the most under-used. It is the bridge from a storefront to a legal person who can sign a contract, and it makes new-business leads possible at all.

sources.name: Better Business Bureau
sources.notes: No public API. Listed because the coverage is genuinely useful for competitor mapping, but it stays off until there is an agreement — a scraper here is a cease-and-desist waiting to happen and the data is not worth it.

sources.name: YellowPages / IYP directories
sources.notes: Largely stale and mostly duplicated by Places. Kept in the registry for the legacy trades that still only list here.

sources.name: Facebook Pages (Graph API)
sources.notes: Public Page data only, never personal profiles. Post cadence is the useful part — a contractor posting three times a week is growing and is a live prospect; one dormant since 2021 usually is not trading.

sources.name: County assessor records
sources.notes: The backbone of every property module. Roughly 3,100 counties, each with its own format and cadence — normalising them is most of the ingest work and most of the defensibility.

sources.name: Building permit records
sources.notes: Highest-intent public data that exists. Also a competitor feed for free — contractorName tells you exactly who is winning work in your ZIP and at what ticket size.

sources.name: Deed and lien records
sources.notes: Drives tenure, equity modelling and the recent-purchase trigger. Public by statute in every state, though a handful are non-disclosure on price.

sources.name: Aerial imagery + CV inference
sources.notes: Inference, not observation. Every field carries its own model confidence and the score weights it accordingly — an unverified guess presented as a fact is how a customer stops trusting the whole product.

sources.name: NOAA storm events
sources.notes: Free, public domain, authoritative. Storm-chasing roofers pay four figures a month for repackaged versions of this exact feed.

sources.name: NOAA/NWS forecast
sources.notes: Turns a static list into a timed one. This is what makes the HVAC emergency signal work.

sources.name: Census ACS block groups
sources.notes: Block-group aggregates only, never individual. Anything derived from it describes a neighbourhood, and the UI must say so — a modelled area figure presented as a fact about a person is both wrong and, used for eligibility, illegal.

sources.name: State insurance rate filings
sources.notes: Public via SERFF and state DOI portals. A filed double-digit increase is a churn event with a date on it — nobody else in this market uses it.

sources.name: Vehicle registration aggregates
sources.notes: Aggregated to block group, never individual. The federal Driver's Privacy Protection Act restricts personal registration data to enumerated purposes and marketing is not one of them, so individual-level use is off the table entirely.

sources.name: USPS CASS / DPV
sources.notes: Runs before anything else. Address standardisation is what makes cross-source matching work at all — 'N Main St' and 'North Main Street' are one property only after CASS says so, and the vacancy flag alone removes a chunk of wasted contacts.

sources.name: Business email discovery
sources.notes: Business addresses at a business domain, verified by MX and SMTP acceptance. No personal inbox harvesting: it is the fastest way to a spam-trap listing, it torches sending reputation for every customer on the shared pool, and CAN-SPAM's harvesting provisions carry aggravated penalties.

sources.name: Business phone append
sources.notes: Line type matters more than the number. Wireless changes what you may legally dial and how, so it is captured at append time rather than guessed later.

sources.name: National + state Do Not Call
sources.notes: Not a feature — a gate. Every phone number is scrubbed before release and re-scrubbed at least every 31 days, which is the TCPA safe-harbour interval. Statutory damages run $500 to $1,500 per call, so one unscrubbed campaign can cost more than the customer's lifetime value several hundred times over.

sources.name: Known-litigator suppression
sources.notes: A small population of serial TCPA plaintiffs seeds numbers specifically to be called. Suppressing them is the cheapest insurance in the entire stack.

sources.name: Account suppression list
sources.notes: The customer's own opt-outs, honoured instantly across every channel and every export. Applied at release time, so a lead already downloaded still disappears from future pulls.
